heterogeneous

het-er-uh-JEE-nee-us -- stress on the fourth syllable, JEE. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Heterogeneous is consisting of dissimilar or very different parts.

The tide pool held a heterogeneous jumble of creatures -- crabs, anemones, snails, and darting silver fish.

Example

For the bridge-building contest, the teacher deliberately mixes each team: a sixth grader with a ninth grader, an artist with a math whiz, a planner with a builder.

Each team is heterogeneous -- made of genuinely different kinds of members gathered into one group. The parts stay distinct from one another; that variety inside the whole is exactly what the word names.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

assorted: Assorted describes a casual mix put together from various sorts -- assorted candies, assorted stickers in a party bag. Heterogeneous is the formal, scientific word for a whole whose parts differ in kind and stay visibly distinct. A gift tin of chocolates is assorted; the word for parts that differ in kind is heterogeneous.

diverse: Diverse celebrates range, especially among people -- a diverse cast, diverse interests -- and usually carries approval. Heterogeneous is neutral and technical: it just reports that a whole is made of genuinely different kinds that stay distinct. You praise a diverse team; you measure a heterogeneous one.

miscellaneous: Miscellaneous means collected with no organizing idea at all -- a drawer of string, coins, and dead batteries. Heterogeneous says the parts differ in kind yet still add up to one recognizable whole. A junk drawer is miscellaneous; a zoo is heterogeneous.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

identical: exactly the same

unvaried: all of one kind, without variety

Where it sits · how unlike the pieces are — varied → heterogeneous → dissimilar

varied vs. heterogeneous: Varied is the everyday, milder word -- a varied menu offers several choices, while a heterogeneous one mixes genuinely different kinds side by side, each part keeping its own distinct character.

dissimilar vs. heterogeneous: Dissimilar sharpens the contrast past heterogeneous: a heterogeneous collection contains different kinds that still form one group, while dissimilar things may share nothing at all -- not even a group to belong to.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — hetero-

root — hetero-: other, different (Greek heteros 'other')

root — gen-

root — gen-: kind, type, birth (Greek genos 'kind, race')

suffix — -eous

suffix — -eous: full of; possessing the qualities of (Latin -osus, via Old French -ous)

Put it together

Put it together: Heterogeneous uses the -eous variant of this unit's suffix family. Greek heteros means 'other, different' and genos means 'kind' -- so heterogeneous means 'possessing the quality of different kinds': a whole whose parts belong to other, unlike types. Its mirror twin homogeneous, taught in this same unit, swaps hetero- for homo- ('same').

Use the root in a new word: genre

Use the root in a new word: genre: The bookstore shelves its novels by genre, from mystery to fantasy to historical fiction.

Root Check

Word Choice

Keep the twins straight by their prefixes: Hetero- means different, homo- means same. A heterogeneous mixture, like trail mix, keeps its different parts visible and distinct; the moment everything blends into one indistinguishable sameness, you have crossed over to homogeneous. Science classes use both words for exactly this contrast.
